review:
Unlike Call of Duty - Black Ops II, this actually gets Afghanistan right. The setting looks like the mountains I flew over and the valley I rucked in. It looks like Afghanistan, it sounds like Afghanistan, and despite the game-isms, does a good job of telling the story.  Little things stand out to me - the visible selector switch from semi to full, the relatively realistic weapons models, the radio chatter and dialogue - as authentic. There are some reality breakers, like a general in a suit during cutscenes or the wrong time period highspeed gofast gear on dudes in a game set in 2001, but I can put them aside and enjoy the atmosphere.

The campaign isn't going to appeal to everyone. It's shorter than some, and it's not full of Michael Bay explosions like the Call of Duty series (which I also own). What makes the single player shine is that it's based on real events. The set pieces (vehicle sections, stand-and-fights) are well presented, and logically flow with the game. There's a sense of being part of a larger picture with the radio chatter between AFOs Neptune and Wolfpack and their boss ('Jimmy,' or COL Drucker in the cutscenes). Your actions make sense, and several times throughout the game you'll see the other AFO doing their part of the missions.

It's worth picking up, on sale or full price, and getting a solid play through. If you want to see a more realistic shooter than the Call of Duty series with a story grounded in actual events, this is the one. This is probably the most under-appreciated military shooter in recent memory for me, purely as an on-the-rails gut wrench adrenaline ride (the downhill scramble to the chopper and the stand-your-ground sequences in particular). Yeah, there's hand-holding, but it the game it makes sense. No one plays rambo in real life, because that's how you die.

This game was slept on. The single player campaign was really fun, stunning graphics, very emotional, very authentic seeming. It made you seem as though you were actually involved in the fight. It's such an shame the series had to die.

As a veteran, I've played through the campaign three times now with a year in between each. It's not a Hollywood blockbuster movie, so don't have an expectation of that.  It's gritty and dirty, and leaves you with mixed emotions that are hard to recognize at the end.  You may feel sad, angry, pissed off, sad again...and ultimately thankful.  All rolled into one.

The story is good, and for me, emotional.  It brings back the memories of camaraderie, of knowing deep down that for your buddies, you'll run through a fusillade of fire in order to drag them out if need be.  For me, it's powerfully moving, and at the end, I just sit and let time take me backwards until it's time to return to the present again.

Functionally, the visuals are somewhat dated, but they work.  The gunplay is as expected for a game and breaks from reality sometimes (no one reloads with the exact same speed, accuracy and deft paws that are chronicled here everytime you do so, it just doesn't happen due to Murphy's Law). The sounds are good, and the voice acting is very convincing.  Most of the major players sound just like you would expect elite operators to sound like.

If you like first-person shooters and a good, albeit short, storyline, pick it up.  Especially if it's on sale for $5 or so.  Worth it.

Medal of Honor (2010) was EA’s attempt to revive the classic franchise and bring it into the modern warfare era. The core gameplay loop is still a classic linear FPS experience: follow objectives, move through different environments, and complete missions involving raids, reconnaissance, sniping, and direct combat.

Compared to Call of Duty, which was already moving toward a more cinematic style at the time, Medal of Honor chose a more documentary-like approach. Unfortunately, this direction was held back by the  writing, which never really left a strong impression.

The game uses multiple playable characters and tries to show modern warfare from different perspectives. However, these characters do not feel very different to play. Most of the gameplay still focuses on small-scale special operations, such as using the environment to move stealthily, working with your squad, and completing objectives with limited resources.

That said, this approach actually fits the theme of the game quite well. This game is not really about being a heroic super soldier. Instead, it focuses more on the exhaustion, confusion, and psychological pressure that come with war. Some missions, especially “Belly of the Beast,” do a great job of creating a feeling of isolation and helplessness on the battlefield, and those moments are genuinely impressive.

However, the game has plenty of problems. The enemy AI is extremely dumb, the tactical depth is very limited, and the game’s scripting is way too restrictive. In some missions, enemies will keep spawning no matter how many you kill until you wait for air support to save you. It makes the combat feel less like a tactical operation and more like following a preset script.

As for the gunplay, whether Medal of Honor or Black Ops has the better shooting system really depends on personal preference.

In the end, Medal of Honor (2010) naturally became another game that was overshadowed by the legendary Call of Duty: Black Ops, along with Battlefield: Bad Company 2. But honestly, I don’t think it was simply a bad game, I mean, It wasn’t defeated by some random FPS, it was competing against some of the most polished and successful shooters from the golden age of FPS games, so its lack of major success was not really surprising. After Medal of Honor: Warfighter failed to revive the series in 2012, the franchise eventually disappeared completely. Looking back today, it is still a little disappointing, because Medal of Honor (2010) had some genuinely great ideas and its own unique identity.

This isn't the best game out there. Not by a long-shot. It's actually THE game that made the world agree that the 'modern military shooter' genre was played out needed to die. The multiplayer is entirely dead and worthless at this point, so that will be ignored, and for the purposes of this review, Medal of Honor 2010 will be treated as a singleplayer-game.

That being said, it is actually one of the better games in the genre. At least if you're looking for something that's more down-to-earth than the various rather ridiculous entries in the Call of Duty franchise. I won't call it realistic, that title is reserved for the likes of ARMA and Squad. But it catches a good atmosphere, presents some fun and satisfying gunplay with the solid, powerful sound-design that EA since has become famous for. 

The story is set during the war in Afghanistan, and you play as American special operations soldiers. That's... About all there is to say about the story. It's not memorable and it's not that powerful, but that doesn't really feel like it's the point of it either. What it does do well is showcase various events and scenarios experienced by special forces in Afghanistan through a loosely-tied storyline to string it together, and it works for that purpose. Most importantly, the story isn't stupid or over-the-top, like Battlefield and Call of Duty tends to be.

It's not the best game, but the graphics more-or-less hold up, the sound design is great, the gunplay is good and it's all grounded in a believable, but bland story. If you're looking for a couple hours of decent FPS gameplay, it's worth a shot. If you're burnt out on the modern military shooter theme, what the hell are you even doing on this store page?

How the brass completely took over the mission and caused major catastrophes that taken the lives of US special operators. Go watch shreks accounts of tora bora, another D boy. I have played this game a few times since it came out, and even here in 2025 it is still in my top ten. As a former U.S. Navy serviceman, I connect with this one in a way I never have with Call of Duty or Battlefield. Those games are great for spectacle, but Medal of Honor feels real.

From the moment it starts, you can tell this game was made with respect. The radio chatter, the way the team moves, the quiet professionalism, it is not about flash or kill counts. It is about brotherhood, the mission, and the cost. The developers worked with actual Tier 1 operators, and you can feel it in every firefight. Nothing feels exaggerated; it feels earned.

The campaign is short, but every mission counts. The mountain fights and night raids are some of the most immersive in any military shooter I have played. And that ending is brutal. It stays with you long after the credits roll. It is not cinematic; it is personal.

I really wish EA had kept this series going, but they stopped supporting it in favor of Battlefield. That is a shame, because there is nothing else like Medal of Honor. It is a grounded, respectful look at modern warfare, and it still holds up beautifully.

If you want a military shooter that feels authentic rather than over the top, this is the one.

Gotta write a nostalgic review. It's been 8 years since this game was released, it's still one of my most fondly remembered FPS-games with MW2 & CS 1.6. Sure, the release wasn't as good as MW2. There were a lot of modern war games coming at the time and MoH got squashed by CoD & BF which is sad. Medal of Honor 2010 & Warfighter were among the finest FPS-games with beautiful campaigns & addictive multiplayer. I was hooked as hell on the multiplayer, played it non-steam version over 200 hours. The campaign was made in Unreal Engine 3 & multiplayer on DICE's Frostbite engine (Bad Company 2 one).

Campaign was short, like 4-5 hours but it still was more emotional & awesomely crafted dare I say... Modern Warfare 1. It didn't skip as hell, flowed beautifully and god damn that Apache mission was awesome. Multiplayer was a mix of Call of Duty & Battlefield. It featured a few vehicles like the Bradley on the US side. Gameplay was top notch and so was the gunplay. Danger Close was a fairly new company trying to take a AAA-franchise. Warfighter followed after MoH 2010 which had a lot of potential but wasn't as good as MoH 2010. After Warfighters low sales and mixed critic, EA (fuck you EA, fuck you) pulled the plug on MoH & Danger Close (fuck you EA, fuck you). 

I truely hope they give this franchise to a good developer (not DICE) that could continue the modern side of Medal of Honor. I recommend these games, they are cheap already, check Warfighter too. The multiplayer is alive on that game.

Medal of Honor 2010 was a strange game when it released back in the day. It was a modern reboot of the whole franchise, which most of the original MoH players did not appreciate. Most of the players and critics called it a shallow run by the mill modern FPS, that was not groundbreaking or innovative in any way. As the time went by. More people started to appreciate it for what it was. You did not play as a group of heroes going all around the world, stopping nuclear threats, surviving things that in our world would be impossible to survive. Every mission was realistic to a point, where you felt that death awaited you at every corner. Missions and story of this reboot was inspired by real life operations performed by actual soldiers. There is no happy ending, where you and your squadmates are celebrated for your victory.  Instead it sends a message, that no matter how many hostiles you eliminate, no matter how big is your victory, their are still losses on both sides in this never-ending conflict between mankind. 

If you want a short, enjoyable campaign, this is the game that I can recommend to people for years to come.  Its just a shame that its sequel, MoH Warfighter, took a sharp turn, going into more spectacular, less realistic missions just to appeal to more mainstream FPS audience. With bad level design, story that was extremely shallow and nothing memorable aside from Castle of Glass by Linkin Park being in its soundtrack. Not to mention that the last time that they tried to revive this franchise was with VR exclusive title with bad jokes and not so serious story.

[b]NOTE:[/b] This review will cover single player only; the multiplayer component of this game is dead and should bear little weight in purchasing decisions. Online servers were shut down on February 22 2023.

The 2010 reboot of Medal of Honor is the series' first foray into modern warfare (all previous titles were set during World War 2). As one would expect, there is a degree of historical accuracy here: the game is loosely based on parts of Operation Anaconda; specifically, the events surrounding the Battle of Roberts Ridge. If you wish to read more, the Wikipedia page is a good place to start ([url]https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Takur_Ghar[/url]).

As one might expect of an FPS set in modern-day theatres, Medal of Honor is rather similar to Battlefield and Call of Duty in terms of feel/look/sound. The focus this time is on realism: real world battle(s), real weapons, real enemies (this game differs in that you are actually fighting the Taliban, rather than some fictional nationalist force - this caused some controversy, especially on US military bases) and of course the ensuing acronyms (I had to ask Google to figure out what SOFLAM stood for). None of these are negatives but equally Medal of Honor does not really do much to distinguish itself from the competition either - it largely follows an already blazed trail without adding too much of its own unique twist on things.

The major complaint pertaining to Medal of Honor is the campaign length: it is SHORT. If you are a competent FPS player, you can expect to complete the entire campaign in roughly 4-5 hours on the hardest difficulty. Similarly once again to Call of Duty (here we reference the first two games), you play from different perspectives as you fill into each faction: the SEALs/Tier 1 operators are more surgical and stealthy in their approach, while the Rangers are gung-ho and aggressive as you might imagine. It can also be a bit generic from an action perspective: there is the "expected" sniper section, as well as a chopper gunner section and a section where you need to call in air support. While not boring or bland and certainly relevant to the story, it does feel a little bit run-of-the-mill as it has been done before elsewhere. Perhaps my biggest gripe however is the linearity: I understand that you have a path to your objective and you may need to funnel players, but suspending your disbelief and being forced down a narrow corridor when you have the wide open spaces of Afghanistan in front of you feels somewhat egregious. With all of this being said though, the campaign is enjoyable and it tells a good story, well paced and varied enough to keep you invested for its rather short length.

In terms of the technical, Medal of Honor gets most of it right. The voice acting is spot on - you can generally hear and feel the frustration and/or relief of your squad mates (end of Belly of the Beast as reference). While the music may not reach the heights of Allied Assault, it is still decent and well chosen to fit the occasions, even if the voice acting is the more emotive audial aspect. Graphically, it seems to be a bit of a mixed bag in 2025: there are areas which held up well, and others which looked poor - although this may have more to do with how I was playing it. Which brings me into the important technical point: performance. There were sections which ran terribly (like 40fps terribly) which for a 15 year old game is not acceptable. Also for reasons which make no sense, there is no option to adjust the FOV. The default is absolutely terrible and makes the movement feel slow and clunky. To address these problems, I recommend going to the PCGamingWiki page ([url]https://www.pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/Medal_of_Honor_(2010)[/url]) and downloading the relevant files. At the very least, you should use the FOV changer as this improved the experience dramatically for me.

If you are interested in playing this, grab it while heavily discounted - the price is simply too high to justify given the length of the campaign. It is enjoyable to play through and I feel it is worth a go on sale, but it cannot be considered a must-play.

Based on the real Battle of Roberts Ridge (Takhur Ghar) where SEAL PO1 Neil Roberts and Air Force Combat Controller TSgt John Chapman both lost their lives fighting alone. The game, despite it's horribly cheesy and sometimes downright bad moments, portrays a solid image of what it might have been like to have been in the Shahi-Kot valley during the early days of the War in Afghanistan. The game has the player playing as members from two different AFO teams from the SEALs and Army Delta Force and as a Ranger from the 75th Ranger Regiment, all of which were present at some point and in some capacity in the real battle. 

One of the shining examples of the brilliance of the story is the failure of inter-unit communications and a contest of command. During the events of the Battle of Roberts Ridge, after the death of Petty Officer Roberts and TSgt Chapman's separation from his unit, the Rangers were sent in despite objection from operational units on the ground. This breakdown of command would see 1 pilot, 1 Pararescueman, and 3 Rangers killed attempting to retrieve Chapman and Roberts. Chapman, despite mortal wounds from Al-Qaeda (AQ) fire, would stand and hold his ground for over an hour while Ranger help was on the way. TSgt Chapman died from his wounds on the mountain after holding off the AQ fighters allowing the Rangers to land without crashing. Chapman was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor by the President on August 22, 2018. 

As for the gameplay, it's relatively generic FPS shooter gameplay that you might expect from a shooter made in 2010. There isn't anything too fancy about and it is functional. It is passable and can make for some very engaging firefights. The story on its own isn't super complex as the point of the AFO teams on Takhur Ghar was mainly to kill enemies and coordinate airstrikes on enemy positions. There are some parallels with the story and the real Battle of Takhur Ghar and if you haven't played the game, I won't spoil it for you. Again the game has some fantastic moments spaced out through the game, but at the same time there are some horribly cheesy and awkward moments spread out within as well. The cast of characters are mostly forgettable and you probably won't grow attached to any of them. For the most part, they all sound the same really and it can be hard to tell one from the other on radio comms. But for a game from 2010, it holds up enough for me to enjoy the story every now and then. Since it's only 4 hours long, I can easily sit and play the entire game in one sitting. Overall, an enjoyable and well made game that doesn't shine in any particular area, but tells a solid story and is an homage to what could be considered the first deadly and costly engagement in the War in Afghanistan.

Medal of Honor is a first-person shooter video game developed by Danger Close Games and EA DICE, published by Electronic Arts.

With War in Afghanistan serving as a setting, story is based on parts of Operation Anaconda that took place six months after 9/11. For the first time in the MOH history you will play as multiple characters, including Tier 1 DEVGRU operator and Apache gunner.

Gameplay as you might have expect involves shooting and completing objectives in order to progress and finish missions-core gameplay of shooters in a shooter, what a surprise huh. Objectives involve capturing and clearing out locations, destroying enemy encampments, hostage rescues and so on. Between ordinary gunfights you have other elements, such as stealth and vehicle section, or a sniping sequence so you shouldn't complain about a lack of variety.
In gunfights you use cover, information plus support from your team and variety of weapons to make your way through. Game features auto-regeneration, so if you get hit you need to hide and wait few second. Keep in mind some covers can be destroyed. You will fight in different enviroments, from abandonned villages where close quarter combat thrive and weapons like shotguns show off their potential (and surprising gore as you can tear enemies limbs) to hills and valleys where precision and long ranged weapons will help.
Gunfights are not as flashy and dynamic as in other titles. Game counts on "realism" which is why fights are slow paced with focus on staying alive and eliminating opponents one by one, clearing out locations rather than being a solo hero who charges in and kills everyone.
Honestly this game in general is like that, you won't have epic chase scenes with orchestral soundtrack, plottwists or nuclear threat. Just an operation and soldier being soldiers, which sticks to the core of Medal of Honor-but now OSS Agents are replaced with Tier 1 Operators.
No doubt it's a big plus of the title considering other games set for the...opposite of what I mentioned. Of course this move has it's consequences too.
You can carry 2 main weapons and a pistol at the same time, with pistol having unlimited ammunition (because reasons) plus grenades. Ammo is not a big factor here, if you run out of it you always can swap to another weapon lying on the ground, to your secondary or pistol, plus there is an ability to ask your comrades so they can give you ammo to your current weapon.
Arsenal in game is based on weapons used during that War, so Operators have M4A1 carbines, M16A4 Assault Rifles, MP7A1 Submachine guns with all sort of attachments, sniper systems and more, while Talibans have different varieties of AKMs, PKMs, Dragunov sniper rifles, launchers and so on. If it is possible you can switch firing mode in weapons!

Entire campaign took me 4 hours long to beat, which I don't have to tell you that, is short as hell. To make matters worse, ending you get is a unsatisfying cliffhanger which continues in Warfighter. And you don't want to play Warfighter.
Gameplay wise there are issues too.
AI is so reactive, they just get to covers and accept their fate unless you will play really stupid aka. full rush them, or if they have a support of machine gun that can destroy your cover so they might have a chance of getting you. Without those, they just sit behind a cover but without covering each other, don't use grenades, don't attempt to flank when it's possible. In few cases where you are the one that defends or runs away, enemies are very scripted-they get to a spot and stand there firing, making those moment a shooting gallery, unfortunately.
Rest of the elements that are "not that good" such as average gunplay, or lack of challenge even on hardest mode make things worse, but all of them need a bit of polish and can become good. Still, you have to count those.

Besides short Single Player campaign, you have a Tier 1 Mode. It's a basic time mode where you have to beat a mission in shortest amount of time, with few additions. You die, you start entire mission again, hardest difficulty mode, headshots and melee kills stop the timer for short amount of time. Fun mode.
Multiplayer is a seperate component, however you should not look at it as it's dead. Dead-dead, MP's monthly peaks are less than 20 players.
Although there is an interesting controversy coming out of it. Modern shooters and controversies go like bread and butter, Modern Warfare 2 "No Russian", Battlefield 3 execution scene, Spec Ops: The Line and white phosphorous, probably there is more but you get the point. Anyway, because as obvious as it is, in Multiplayer one has to play as good guys, one as bad guys, and in game bad guys are Talibans, meaning same in MP. Some people found it disturbing, that you can recreate crimes by them in game, and it's not something for children (Wow could it be M rated game is not for kids?). Group of such people includes UK Defence Secretary, Canadian Defense Minister, Danish Defense Minister, and majority of US Military. Devs replaced word "Talibans" with the term "OpFor" (Opposive Force). It didn't affect singleplayer nor gameplay but game because of that is still banned for sale on military bases, even to this day. Wack. 

You won't find any controversies in terms of performance, game runs on smooth 60 frames per second like it should, and without any problems with textures, glitches crashes etc.

4-5 hours short but very sweet single player campaign that shows it was created with the help of soldiers that served in Afghanistan. Lots of military jargon and an astonishing variety of mission types. You sweep villages, infiltrate, control drones, lay fire from helicopters or try to run away from overwhelming hordes of enemies. Missions are well connected as you take control of different soldiers from a different unit after each mission. 

This game manages to convey the nitty gritty feel of boots on the ground. Many missions could be taken straight out of Marcus Luttrell's "Lone Survivor" book. 

The sound track is very good, especially in those missions where you fight against all odds. Gun sounds sometime lack the oomp but friendly air support totally makes up for that.

The graphics still hold up to this day...
Story is nicely presented (Based on Operation Anaconda)...

Everything's good except the game length.

After Call of Duty moved to modern times, it was the first game set in modern times by Medal of Honor. The subject they chose was good, it was about the operations of American Navy Seal commandos in Afghanistan and they wrote a good story. They were probably inspired by the true story in the Lone Survivor movie. Later, they finished the story very well with the sequel Moh Warfighter and it was a very good game.

This game holds a special place in my heart, despite it being a short campaign it has a really gritty take on the GWOT and feels like it was made for veterans who served during that time, They were able to do such a good job with the software they had at the time that it still hold up to this day. highly recommend for a quick old school FPS with a great story if you ever see this on sale for cheap. i wish EA still made campaign stories like this.
